title: Binary search
summary: Halve a sorted range in O(log n) without breaking the loop invariant.

parts.rule: Halve a sorted search space while preserving a clear invariant about where the answer can still live. On each step compute mid, then discard the half that cannot contain the answer. Stop when the window collapses to the answer or becomes empty. State whether you want any match, the first true, or the last false before writing the updates to low and high.
parts.why: Once input is ordered, interviewers expect logarithmic search. The usual failures are a mid that never moves, off-by-one exits, and returning mid without checking the predicate the prompt actually asked for. Saying the invariant out loud catches those before the loop is typed.
parts.example: Find the first index of value 7 in sorted array [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]. Invariant: answer lies in [low, high] if it exists. Start low=0, high=4. Mid=(0+4)//2=2, a[2]=5, which is less than 7, so the answer cannot be at mid or left — set low=mid+1=3. Now low=3, high=4. Mid=(3+4)//2=3, a[3]=7, which satisfies "value >= 7" for a lower_bound style search, so set high=mid=3. Now low=high=3. Confirm a[3]==7 and return 3. Every iteration either raised low or lowered high, so the window shrank and the answer stayed inside it. If the target were 6 (absent), the same lower_bound walk ends at the insertion point index 3.
parts.use: Use binary search on a sorted array for exact hit or lower/upper bound. Use it on a numeric range when a monotonic predicate becomes true and stays true. Use it for first-true / last-false boundaries after you can state that predicate in one sentence.
parts.refuse: Refuse binary search on unsorted input. Refuse a loop that can leave low and high unchanged for a full iteration. Refuse returning mid just because values matched once without checking whether the prompt wanted the first, last, or any occurrence. Refuse binary search when a linear scan of tiny n is clearer and asymptotics do not matter.

body:
Rule. Halve a sorted search space while preserving a clear invariant about where the answer can still live. On each step compute mid, then discard the half that cannot contain the answer. Stop when the window collapses to the answer or becomes empty. State whether you want any match, the first true, or the last false before writing the updates to low and high.

Why it matters. Once input is ordered, interviewers expect logarithmic search. The usual failures are a mid that never moves, off-by-one exits, and returning mid without checking the predicate the prompt actually asked for. Saying the invariant out loud catches those before the loop is typed.

Worked example. Find the first index of value 7 in sorted array [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]. Invariant: answer lies in [low, high] if it exists. Start low=0, high=4. Mid=(0+4)//2=2, a[2]=5, which is less than 7, so the answer cannot be at mid or left — set low=mid+1=3. Now low=3, high=4. Mid=(3+4)//2=3, a[3]=7, which satisfies "value >= 7" for a lower_bound style search, so set high=mid=3. Now low=high=3. Confirm a[3]==7 and return 3. Every iteration either raised low or lowered high, so the window shrank and the answer stayed inside it. If the target were 6 (absent), the same lower_bound walk ends at the insertion point index 3.

When to use. Use binary search on a sorted array for exact hit or lower/upper bound. Use it on a numeric range when a monotonic predicate becomes true and stays true. Use it for first-true / last-false boundaries after you can state that predicate in one sentence.

When to refuse. Refuse binary search on unsorted input. Refuse a loop that can leave low and high unchanged for a full iteration. Refuse returning mid just because values matched once without checking whether the prompt wanted the first, last, or any occurrence. Refuse binary search when a linear scan of tiny n is clearer and asymptotics do not matter.
